Dockerfile.text:
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
# Static site: the page, its modules and the guides. Tests stay out of the image.
COPY index.html calc.mjs usage.mjs robots.txt sitemap.xml *-*.html /usr/share/nginx/html/
RUN printf 'types { text/javascript mjs; }\n' > /etc/nginx/conf.d/mjs.conf
EXPOSE 80
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/ >/dev/null || exit 1

README.md.text:
# Container Load Planner

Free, browser-only 3D load planner for small exporters, Amazon/FBA and DTC
sellers shipping cartons or pallets. List cargo lines (size, weight, quantity,
rotation, highest layer, weight allowed on top), pick a 20 ft, 40 ft, 40 ft high
cube, 53 ft trailer, 26 ft box truck, standard pallet or your own size, and it
reports what fits, what is left over, volume and weight use, how many containers
the whole load needs, a to-scale top and side view and a loading list. A "what if
I swap" table runs the same cargo through every standard size, loose and on
pallets. Metric or imperial. Nothing is uploaded.

**Live tool:** https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/container-load-planner/

Open `index.html`. No build step, no dependencies. `node --test` runs the suite.

- `calc.mjs` - parsing and units, the extreme-point 3D packer (orientation,
  support, layer and load-on-top constraints, payload), seeded multi-start
  search, greedy multi-container planning with tail consolidation, palletising,
  the container comparison, view geometry, and an independent `verifyPacking`
  checker.
- Printable load plan: one self-contained HTML file (no script) with a to-scale top and side SVG per container, the ordered-versus-packed table, the balance check, the loading list and the disclaimer, to print to PDF for the warehouse or the forwarder (`planReportHtml`).
- Share link: `encodeShare`/`decodeShare` put the whole form in the URL hash (`#plan=...`) so a plan can be sent to a forwarder or colleague; nothing is stored on a server.
- Freight quotes in the page: type what each container size was quoted (`20ft=2400, 40ft=3800`) under "What if I swap?" and the table adds the total and cost per unit for the whole load, marking the cheapest option that fits everything (`priceOptions`, same as the CLI's `--rates`). The tool ships no rates of its own.
- Command line: `cli.mjs` runs the same packer on a cargo CSV with no browser and no network, for forwarders and ops scripts that plan many shipments. Zero dependencies.

  ```
  node cli.mjs cargo.csv                       # containers needed, fit, balance (40 ft by default)
  node cli.mjs --container 20ft cargo.csv      # 20ft, 40ft, 40hc, 53ft, truck26
  node cli.mjs --container 589x235x239@28200 cargo.csv   # your own inside size (cm) and payload (kg)
  node cli.mjs --compare cargo.csv             # every standard size, loose and on pallets
  node cli.mjs --rates 20ft=2400,40ft=3800 cargo.csv   # freight at your quoted rates: total and cost per carton, cheapest complete option marked
  node cli.mjs --csv cargo.csv > loading.csv   # loading list
  node cli.mjs --html cargo.csv > plan.html    # printable to-scale plan
  node cli.mjs --json cargo.csv                # for scripts; add --imperial for inches and pounds
  ```

  Cargo lines are `name, length, width, height, weight, quantity[, rotation, highest layer, weight on top, delivery stop]`; give lines a stop number (1 is unloaded first) for a multi-drop run and the packer loads the last stop deepest, then reports any unit left behind cargo for a later stop (`stopReport`); `--example` runs the invented sample.
- `usage.mjs` - local-only feature counters with an opt-out.
- `how-to-plan-a-container-load.html` - guide with a worked example that the
  test suite recomputes.

## What you use today, and what this does differently

- **A spreadsheet of cubic metres:** quick, but total volume ignores carton shapes, rotation limits, stacking and weight, so it overstates what fits.
- **Freight forwarder or carrier quotes and their load calculators:** accurate for their own booking, but usually need contact details and are tied to a quote. This tool needs no signup and states no rate.
- **Desktop and paid load-planning software:** deeper (axle weights, bracing, carrier rules), and priced and set up for logistics teams. This tool is for the earlier question of how many containers to book.
- **What this adds:** a to-scale 3D packing with rotation, support and load-on-top rules, an independent checker of each plan, a swap table across standard container sizes, a centre-of-gravity check (back-heavy, side-heavy or top-heavy loads are flagged), and a loading list. Nothing is uploaded.

**No warranty.** Free and as-is; a planning aid, not legal, tax, financial or
safety advice, and not a load-securing, axle-weight or compliance certificate.
It reports the centre of gravity (assuming evenly loaded units) but does not model bracing, axle weights, pallet overhang,
dunnage, hazardous goods or carrier limits, and states no freight rate. The
packer is a heuristic: it tries many orderings and keeps the best, which is not
a proof of optimality. Container sizes and payloads are nominal and editable.
Unverified against a real loading: tested on hand-computed fits and on random
loads checked for overlap, bounds, weight, rotation, support and stacking.

**Privacy.** Everything runs in your browser; your figures are never uploaded.
Anonymous feature counts stay in local storage and can be switched off.

MIT licence, see `LICENSE`.

## Host your own copy

Your data stays in your browser either way, but you can serve the page from an address you control. It is a static
site: the server only hands out files and never sees a figure or a file you load.

- **Docker:** `docker compose up -d`, then open <http://localhost:8080> (`Dockerfile` is nginx plus the page's files).
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch --copy-config --no-deploy --dockerfile Dockerfile`, then `fly deploy` (`fly.toml`).
- **Render:** deploy from your fork with `render.yaml` (static site, no paid plan needed).
- Nothing runs on the author's accounts. The Docker image has not been built in the session that added these files,
  so build it once and open the page before relying on it. Tests: `node --test deploy.test.mjs`.

name: container-load-planner
description: >-
  Free browser tool for small exporters, Amazon/FBA and DTC sellers shipping
  cartons or pallets: enter cargo lines with size, weight, quantity, rotation and
  stacking limits, pick a 20 ft, 40 ft, 40 ft high cube, 53 ft trailer, box truck,
  pallet or custom size, and a 3D packing heuristic shows what fits, what is left
  over, how many containers the whole load needs, a to-scale top and side view and
  a loading list, and compares other containers and pallets. Nothing leaves the
  browser.
stage: prototype
owner: duncan

# Screened 2026-10-01 in a new-venture session asked for a deeper, algorithmic
# tool. duplicate_check.py (re-run before commit): closest rows were
# amazon-fba-calculator 0.20 (fees, not loading), fba-aged-inventory-fee-analyzer
# 0.15 and fba-reimbursement-claim-finder 0.15 (unrelated), and a screened-out row
# for local-business websites / print-on-demand 0.15 (unrelated); nothing near the
# 0.45 line. Existing neighbours by hand: shipping-box-size-optimizer (which carton
# sizes to stock, cross-linked), parcel-dim-weight-calculator (one carton),
# ltl-freight-class-estimator (one pallet's class) and liquidation-pallet-bid-
# calculator (bidding on pallets). None packs a load into a container.
#
# Why this niche: a small exporter, an Amazon FBA seller sending a pallet shipment
# or a DTC brand moving stock to a 3PL has to answer "will it fit, and how many
# containers or trucks?" before it books space. Load-planning software
# (cube optimisation, "cargo loading" tools) is sold to forwarders and shippers at
# enterprise prices; the small shipper gets a rule of thumb and a surprise at the
# dock. This tool does the real 3D packing with rotation, weight and stacking
# limits and shows it to scale.
#
# First visitor: people searching "how many pallets fit in a 40ft container",
# "container load calculator", "will my cartons fit in a 20ft container", plus
# FBA and export forums when a booking is being planned. Volume not measured with
# an external tool.
#
# Liability boundary: arithmetic and a packing heuristic on user-typed figures; a
# planning aid, not a load-securing, axle-weight or legal certificate; no freight
# rate asserted; container sizes and payloads are nominal, editable and labelled
# as such; the example cargo is invented and says so.
#
# Path to revenue (payment rails stay off): lead magnet and donations; a natural
# front end for a hosted multi-shipment planner or forwarder quote request.

hypotheses:
  - claim: >-
      Small shippers will use a private, no-signup container load planner when
      they plan a booking, and the to-scale view and container comparison change
      the container size or the number of containers they book.
    status: untested
    checked: null
    evidence: customer-contact

economics:
  currency: USD
  mrr: null
  monthly_cost: 0
  customers: null

budget:
  monthly_cap: 1
  protected: true

kill_criteria:
  - Fewer than three distinct GitHub users (issues, stars, or a paste-in report) engage with the tool within 90 days of it being reachable from the published site.
  - A user reports that a plan places units that overlap, exceed the payload or break a stacking limit they entered.

links:
  production: https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/container-load-planner/
  analytics: null

docker-compose.yml.text:
# Any box with Docker:  docker compose up -d   (then open http://localhost:8080)
# Put a TLS proxy in front for a public address. Nothing you type reaches the server: it only serves files.
services:
  container-load-planner:
    build: .
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports: ["8080:80"]

fly.toml.text:
# Fly.io self-deploy, in your own account (needs flyctl):
#   fly launch --copy-config --no-deploy --dockerfile Dockerfile
#   fly deploy
app = "container-load-planner-CHANGE-ME"
primary_region = "iad"

[build]
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 80
  force_https = true
  auto_stop_machines = "stop"
  auto_start_machines = true
  min_machines_running = 0

how-to-plan-a-container-load.html.text:
← Container load planner

How to plan a container load, with a worked example

Before you book space, you want to know how many cartons or pallets go in a container, and how many containers the whole load needs. The answer is set by four things: the floor area, how many layers fit under the roof, what you may stack on what, and the payload limit. Whichever runs out first sets the count.

Open the free container load planner

The four limits

Floor. Count how many footprints fit across the width and along the length, trying both ways round. Odd widths waste floor: two 120 cm Euro pallets side by side do not fit a 235 cm interior, so loaders mix pallet directions, and that is what a packer has to search for.

Layers. Divide the inside height by the unit height, rounded down. A 110 cm pallet gets two layers under a 239 cm roof and wastes 19 cm; an 85 cm pallet gets two layers in a standard 40 ft and three in a high cube, because three times 85 is 255 and the high cube is about 270 cm tall.

Stacking. Cartons marked fragile or pallets of soft goods may not be stacked, so the layer count becomes one. The planner takes a highest layer and a weight allowed on top for each line.

Payload. A dense load fills the payload before the space. A 600 kg pallet in a 26,500 kg container stops at 44 pallets however much air is left.

A worked example

An invented exporter has 150 Euro pallets, each 120 × 80 × 85 cm and 250 kg, which may be stacked. The planner uses nominal inside sizes of 12,032 × 2,352 × 2,393 mm for a 40 ft container and 2,698 mm high for the high cube, both with a 26,500 kg payload. These are commonly quoted figures, not a certificate for your equipment.

ContainerPallets in the firstLayersContainers for 150
40 ft5023
40 ft high cube7532

The floor takes 25 pallets in both, in a mixed arrangement of lengthwise and crosswise rows. The standard container stops at two layers, 50 pallets, so 150 pallets need three of them. The high cube takes a third layer, 75 pallets, so two of them carry everything, at 18,750 kg each, well inside the payload.

Change the pallet height to 110 cm and the extra height buys nothing: three layers need 330 cm, so a high cube still holds two layers and 50 pallets. Whether a high cube pays depends on the cargo, not on the container alone.

Now make the pallets 600 kg and 110 cm tall, 70 of them, in a standard 40 ft. The floor and the two layers would take 50, but the payload stops the first container at 44 pallets (26,400 kg); the remaining 26 pallets go in a second container, 15,600 kg. Two containers, and the lower bound from weight is also two.

What the planner does that a rule of thumb does not

  1. It packs mixed lines, so a pallet and four sizes of carton share one container and fill each other's gaps.
  2. It respects rotation: upright only, any orientation, or fixed as entered.
  3. It reports what is left over, how many containers the whole load needs, a lower bound from volume and weight, and a to-scale top and side view with a loading list.
  4. It compares every standard size, loose and on pallets, so the high cube and the pallet question get an answer for your own cargo.

It is a heuristic: it tries many orderings and keeps the best, which is not a proof that nothing better exists. A person who knows the cargo may find another fit, so keep a margin.

Common questions

How many pallets fit in a 20 ft container?

A nominal 20 ft container is about 5.9 m long and 2.35 m wide, so its floor holds about 11 Euro pallets or 10 of the 48 x 40 inch size, and a second layer doubles that if the pallets are low and strong enough to stack. The planner packs your own pallet size and weight rather than quoting a number.

Does a high cube container always hold more?

No. It adds about 30 cm of height, which helps only when a whole extra layer fits. Three layers of 85 cm pallets fit a high cube but not a standard container; three layers of 110 cm fit neither.

Why does weight sometimes decide the count?

A container has a payload limit. Dense goods such as 600 kg pallets reach it long before the space is used, so the number per container is the payload divided by the weight per unit, rounded down.

Should I palletise or load cartons loose?

Pallets are faster to load and handle, but each deck takes height and the pallet footprint can waste floor. Compare both on your own cargo; the planner's comparison table shows containers and fill for each.

Choosing carton sizes before you pack? The shipping box size optimizer picks which sizes to stock. Shipping a single pallet by LTL? The LTL freight class estimator works out the class.

No warranty. Free and as-is. Not legal, tax, financial, safety or shipping advice, and not a load-securing, axle-weight or compliance certificate. The example exporter, cargo and container figures are invented or nominal and may differ from your equipment; carrier and forwarder rules change. Verify the output with your carrier, forwarder or a qualified loading supervisor; you remain responsible for decisions made from it. No data is uploaded.

Use the planner · Licence · GitHub Sponsors

index.html.text:
CONTAINER LOAD PLANNER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Will it fit in the container?

List your cartons or pallets with size, weight and quantity, pick a 20 ft, 40 ft, 40 ft high cube, 53 ft trailer, box truck, pallet or your own size, and see what fits, what is left over and how many containers the whole load needs, with a to-scale top and side view and a loading list.

A planning aid, not a load-securing, axle-weight or legal certificate. New to this? Read how to plan a container load, with a worked example.

1. Units and container

2. Your cargo

Rotation: upright keeps the height you enter vertical (it may turn on its vertical axis), any allows all six orientations, fixed keeps it exactly as entered. Highest layer 1 means floor only. Max on top is the most weight that may rest on one unit; 0 means nothing on top. Leave a box blank for no limit.

Pallet settings, for the “pack on pallets” comparison

Add your cargo and pick a container, then click Plan the load.

#ContentsUnitsVolume usedWeight% of payload

The link holds your cargo and container in its address, so anyone who opens it sees the same inputs. It is never sent to a server by this tool; whoever you send it to can read it.

What if I swap?

The same cargo through every standard size, loose and on pallets. Container counts and fill only; it states no rate of its own. Type the quotes you have been given (one container each) and the table adds what the whole load costs.

OptionContainersAverage fillLast containerYour costNote

How it is calculated

Packing: a constructive 3D bin packing heuristic with extreme-point placement. Units go in one at a time at the lowest free corner where they are inside the walls, overlap nothing, and rest on the floor or on units below with at least 75% of their base supported. Each is slid back against the walls and neighbours. The search repeats with three corner rules and several unit orderings, including seeded random ones, and keeps the packing with the most packed volume, then the most units. It is repeatable: the same input gives the same plan.

Constraints: allowed rotations, highest layer, weight allowed on top (spread over the units underneath in proportion to the area they carry) and the payload limit. A separate checker re-verifies every plan for bounds, overlap, payload, orientation, support, layers and load before it is drawn.

Whole load: one container at a time, then what is left, then an attempt to merge the last two. The lower bound is the larger of total volume over container volume and total weight over payload.

Not modelled: load securing and bracing, axle and gross weights, pallet overhang, the true centre of gravity of unevenly loaded units, dunnage and gaps for lashing, door and forklift clearances, hazardous or temperature-controlled goods, carrier or legal limits, and rates. Container sizes and payloads are nominal figures you can edit; check your equipment. Unverified against a real loading: tested on hand-computed fits and on random loads checked for overlap, bounds, weight and rotation.

Common questions

How many pallets fit in a 40 ft container?

It depends on the pallet size, its height and whether it may be stacked. Euro pallets (120 x 80 cm) fit about 25 on the floor of a nominal 40 ft container, in a mix of lengthwise and crosswise rows, so about 50 if they can be stacked two high; 48 x 40 inch pallets fit about 20 on the floor. A nominal 20 ft container takes about 11 Euro pallets or 10 of the 48 x 40 size on the floor. Enter your own pallet size, weight and stacking limit and the planner packs it rather than quoting a rule of thumb.

How does the planner pack a container?

It is a constructive 3D bin packing heuristic. Units are placed one at a time at the lowest free corner where they stay inside the walls, overlap nothing, rest on the floor or on units below with at least 75 percent of the base supported, respect the rotations each line allows, and keep the weight under the payload. Each placement is slid against the walls and neighbours. The search repeats that with different corner rules and unit orderings, including seeded random ones, and keeps the packing with the most volume, then the most units.

Is this the best possible packing?

Not guaranteed. Optimal 3D packing is an NP-hard problem, so the planner is a heuristic that tries many orderings and keeps the best; on regular loads it often finds a perfect fit, on awkward mixes it can leave a little room that a skilled loader would use. Treat the unit counts as a planning estimate and keep a margin.

What do upright only, can rotate and highest layer mean?

Upright only keeps the height you entered vertical and lets the unit turn on its vertical axis. Can rotate allows all six orientations. Fixed keeps the unit exactly as entered. Highest layer is the highest level a unit may sit at, with 1 meaning floor only. Weight allowed on top is the most weight that may rest on one unit, counting everything above it; 0 means nothing may be put on it.

How many containers do I need for the whole load?

The planner fills one container at a time, then repeats on what is left, and reports the number of containers, how full each is, and a lower bound from total volume and total weight. It then tries to merge the last two containers into one. Because it is a heuristic the count may be one higher than the best possible; the lower bound shows how close it is.

What does swapping to a 40 ft high cube or to pallets change?

The comparison runs the same cargo through every standard size and through pallets. A high cube adds height, which helps only if your units can stack. Palletising packs your cartons onto 48 x 40 inch pallets within a height cap, then packs the loaded pallets into each container; it usually costs some volume to the pallet deck but makes the load faster to handle. The table shows the container count and fill for each so you can weigh it against your own quotes.

Does this check that my load is safe or legal?

No. It is a planning aid. It reports where the centre of gravity falls, assuming each unit is evenly loaded, against planning tolerances you should replace with your carrier's. It does not check load securing, axle weights, pallet overhang, hazardous goods rules, or any road, rail, sea or air limit, and it uses nominal container sizes that you can edit. Your carrier, forwarder or loading supervisor decides what can be shipped.

Is my cargo list uploaded?

No. The planner runs in your browser from figures you type, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline after the page loads.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, financial or safety advice, is not a load-securing, axle-weight or regulatory compliance certificate, and does not replace your carrier, forwarder or a qualified loading supervisor. Results are a planning estimate from the figures you type; container sizes and payloads vary by equipment. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output.

Independent. Not affiliated with any shipping line, carrier, forwarder, marketplace or equipment maker, and none is named or ranked here. The example cargo is invented, and no freight rate is stated or implied.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

Everything runs in your browser. Your figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (plan_run, example_loaded, report_downloaded, packet_downloaded, rates_priced) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

Related tools: the shipping box size optimizer for choosing carton sizes, the warehouse slotting optimizer for deciding which shelf each SKU belongs on, the dimensional weight calculator for one parcel, the LTL freight class estimator for pallets, the import landed cost calculator and the 3PL quote normalizer.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

render.yaml.text:
# One-click self-deploy: https://render.com/deploy?repo=<your fork URL>
# Render serves the files as a static site in YOUR account; nothing runs on the author's.
services:
  - type: web
    name: container-load-planner
    runtime: static
    rootDir: ventures/container-load-planner
    staticPublishPath: .
    buildCommand: "true"
    headers:
      - path: /*.mjs
        name: Content-Type
        value: text/javascript
